messages.content: I'm 25 years old and working as a sales executive at a private company in Noida for the past 11 months. My monthly salary is ₹28,000, but my employer hasn't paid me for the last two months. Every time I ask HR, they say the company is facing financial problems and that I'll get my money soon. I have rent and EMIs to pay, and it's becoming really difficult to manage. What can I do to get my salary?

### What you can do today

1. Write to HR and the company’s authorised contact. List each unpaid month, the salary due for it, any amount already paid, and the total still owed; ask for payment by a specific date and request a written response. Keep a copy and proof that you sent it.

2. If both full months are unpaid at ₹28,000 per month, show ₹56,000 as the amount claimed, adjusting for any partial payments or other amounts actually due. Take your written demand, appointment letter or other proof of employment, salary slips, bank statements, and messages from HR to the labour office for Noida and ask which notified wage-claim authority handles your case and how to file there.

3. If you share the two unpaid months and your main work duties, I can help you prepare a clear salary-demand message and organise the amount claimed.

### Keep these ready

Keep original salary records, bank statements and HR messages unchanged, and make dated copies. If the labour office says it is not the correct forum, ask it to identify the proper authority for your role and claim before filing elsewhere.

### One thing that would help me

What are your main duties as a sales executive, including whether you supervise staff or make management decisions? Your role and duties may help identify which authority to ask about your claim.

### What I can't confirm yet

I could not verify the current Noida filing channel. The available routing guidance says the appropriate forum can depend on the workplace location and your role and duties, but it does not establish that managerial duties exclude you from a particular wage-claim route.

sources.text:
In India, the appropriate forum for recovering unpaid salary or full-and-final dues depends on (1) the state/location of the establishment and workplace, (2) the worker's role, duties, supervisory/managerial authority and wage level (determining 'workman' / employee coverage under labour statutes vs civil/summary recovery), and (3) any valid arbitration or jurisdiction clause in the appointment contract; employment wage claims are not consumer disputes.

Exact official passage: NALSA helps individuals access legal aid through different Legal Services Institutions such as SLSAs/DLSAs, if they meet the eligibility criteria under Section 12 and 13 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, and encourages Pre-Institution Mediation and Lok Adalat mechanisms where applicable.

messages.content: The problem is that I never received a proper appointment letter. I only have WhatsApp conversations with HR confirming my salary, previous bank transfers, and attendance records. Yesterday, when I asked my manager about the pending ₹56,000, he got angry and told me that if I complained to the Labour Department, he'd fire me and make sure I didn't get an experience letter. Can they actually do that? And can I still file a complaint without an appointment letter?

**You can approach the Noida labour office with the records you have, but I can’t confirm that they satisfy the filing requirements without an appointment letter.** Section 45 says an employee may apply to the authority appointed to hear wage claims; it does not specify what documents that authority requires. Take your WhatsApp salary messages, bank-transfer records and attendance records, and ask the office which authority handles your claim and whether it will accept these as proof of employment and salary. [1](#cite-1)

### What I'd suggest

For the wage claim, the Code provides for an application to the authority appointed by the government. The employee can apply within three years of the claim arising; the authority may order compensation as well as the wages, and must endeavour to decide within three months. The exact filing authority and method for your Noida workplace still need confirmation. [1](#cite-1)[2](#cite-2)

### What you can do today

1. Write to HR and the company in a calm, factual message: list the two unpaid months, the ₹56,000 claimed, and ask them to confirm when they will pay. Keep a copy and proof it was sent. You can also tell the Noida labour office that you have no appointment letter and ask which notified wage-claim authority handles your case and how to file; if it says it cannot take the claim, ask it to identify the correct authority.

2. I can help you draft the written salary demand to HR using the details you’ve shared.

### If that doesn't work

If the company does dismiss you, keep any written notice and record the date and reason given. Ask the labour office promptly which route covers both the unpaid salary and the dismissal, because the right forum can depend on your duties and role.

### Keep these ready

Keep the WhatsApp chats, bank statements showing earlier salary payments, attendance records, and the manager’s threat message if it was sent in writing. Save original records and make dated copies; note the date and words used if the threat was spoken. These records can help explain your work, salary and what happened.

### What I can't confirm yet

Whether your manager can lawfully dismiss you or withhold an experience letter depends on the facts and rules that apply to your job. I could not verify the specific Uttar Pradesh rules on retaliation or an experience-letter entitlement, so I can’t confirm that either action would be lawful or unlawful.

sources.title: Code on Wages, 2019
sources.locator: Section 45: Claims under Code and procedure thereof
sources.text:
45. (1) The appropriate Government may, by notification, appoint one or more authorities, not below the rank of a Gazetted Officer, to hear and determine the claims which arises under the provisions of this Code. 
(2) The authority appointed under sub-section (1), while deciding the claim under that sub-section, may order, having regard to the circumstances under which the claim arises, the payment of compensation in addition to the claim determined, which may extend to ten times of the claim determined and endeavour shall be made by the authority to decide the claim within a period of three months. 
(3) If an employer fails to pay the claim determined and compensation ordered to be paid under sub-section (2), the authority shall issue a certificate of recovery to the Collector or District Magistrate of the district where the establishment is located who shall recover the same as arrears of land revenue and remit the same to the authority for payment to the concerned employee. 
(4) Any application before the authority for claim referred to in sub-section (1) may be filed by,–– 
(a) the employee concerned; or 
(b) any Trade Union registered under the Trade Unions Act, 1926 of which the employee is a member; or 
(c) the Inspector-cum-Facilitator. 
(5) Subject to such rules as may be made, a single application may be filed under this section on behalf or in respect of any number of employees employed in an establishment. 
(6) The application under sub-section (4) may be filed within a period of three years from the date on which claims referred to in sub-section (1) arises: 
Provided that the authority referred to in sub-section (1) may, entertain the application after three years on sufficient cause being shown by the applicant for such delay. 
(7) The authority appointed under sub-section (1) and the appellate authority appointed under sub-section (1) of section 49, shall have all the powers of a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, for the purpose of taking evidence and of enforcing the attendance of witnesses and compelling the production of documents, and every such authority or appellate authority shall be deemed to be a civil court for all the purposes of section 195 and Chapter XXVI of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

messages.content: ordered three fans from Amazon. Two were the wrong colour, so I requested returns for both. Support registered only one return, but my father handed both fans to the pickup agent, who accepted them. I received only one refund. Support repeatedly promised to arrange the remaining refund, but later closed the investigation because their records showed only one returned item. I also emailed the grievance team, who redirected me to regular support. I have emails, call history and refund assurances. suggest the next practical step..

That is a frustrating loop, especially when your father says the pickup agent accepted both fans. Your next step is to lodge a grievance with the National Consumer Helpline (NCH), rather than being sent back to regular Amazon support again.

### What I'd suggest

For the Amazon refund: You can submit the grievance through the National Consumer Helpline portal or call 1915. NCH forwards the complaint to the company for a response; it is a pre-litigation route, not a court, and it does not guarantee a refund. [1](#cite-1)

### What you can do today

In your grievance, state that two fans were handed to the pickup agent, only one refund arrived, and Amazon closed the investigation because its records showed one return. Ask Amazon to investigate the missing item and issue the remaining refund; include your order number and the amount as needed.

### If that doesn't work

If NCH does not resolve it to your satisfaction, you can file a formal consumer complaint with the District Consumer Commission through e-Jagriti, if the paid consideration is within that Commission’s ₹50 lakh limit. The general filing limit is two years from when the cause of action arose; an NCH grievance does not pause that period. [1](#cite-1)[2](#cite-2)

### Keep these ready

Attach or keep ready the order and return details, proof of the refund already received, emails containing Amazon’s refund assurances and investigation closure, and your call history. Ask your father to write down when and where he handed over both fans and anything he remembers about the pickup agent; this may help explain the mismatch in Amazon’s records.

messages.content: I'm 20 years old and my girlfriend is also 20. We booked an OYO hotel in Patna for a night because we wanted some private time together. Both of us have valid Aadhaar cards, and the hotel allowed us to check in. But after around an hour, the hotel manager knocked on our door and started questioning us about whether we're married. He said unmarried couples aren't allowed to stay together and asked us to leave immediately. Is it actually illegal for us to stay in a hotel together?

**No—based on what you’ve described, two consenting 20-year-olds staying together in a hotel is not, by itself, a crime just because they aren’t married.** The Supreme Court has recognised that consenting adults can live together outside marriage; a High Court has also specifically said that an unmarried adult couple’s occupation of a hotel room is not itself a criminal offence. [1] [1](#cite-1)[2](#cite-2)

---

### What I'd suggest

The specific hotel-room ruling is from the Madras High Court, so it is persuasive rather than binding in Patna. The Supreme Court ruling on consenting adults is binding, but a hotel’s separate booking terms may still matter to a dispute about the booking or a refund. [1] [1](#cite-1)[2](#cite-2)

---

### What you can do today

1. Being allowed to check in and then questioned about marriage sounds unsettling. Keep your booking confirmation, payment proof, and screenshots of the booking terms; note when the manager spoke to you and what was said. [segment:seg-1]

2. If you’re still at the hotel, calmly ask the manager to show you the booking rule they’re relying on and to put any demand that you leave in writing. You can also contact OYO through the booking app and keep a record of the complaint. Don’t physically argue or resist; if you leave, ask OYO about a refund for the unused stay, but the booking terms may affect that.

---

### What I can't confirm yet

I can’t tell from your message whether the booking terms let the hotel end your stay or whether you’re owed a refund. That depends on the terms you accepted and whether you had to leave. [segment:seg-1]

---

### When a lawyer would help

If you share what the booking terms say and whether you had to leave, I can help you work out the next step or draft a message to OYO.

Consenting adults have the right to live together in a live-in relationship outside marriage even if one adult has not yet reached the statutory minimum marriageable age for a male (21 years), and their personal liberty cannot be curtailed merely because they are unmarried or below marriageable age while being major (>=18).

Exact official passage: Both the appellants are major. Even if they were not competent to enter into wedlock, they have right to live together even outside wedlock. Freedom of choice is guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution of India.
sources.limitations: Binding Supreme Court precedent; specifically addresses consenting majors (>=18, including 20-year-old adults) living or associating together outside marriage. Exceptions: Private hotel contractual check-in policies (e.g., valid government ID or disclosed age policy on booking) are civil/consumer contract terms, distinct from criminal illegality Treatment: good_law_editor_verified.

sources.text:
Directly addressing hotel accommodation, the Madras High Court held that the occupation of a hotel room by an unmarried couple of consenting adults is not a criminal offence under Indian law and cannot by itself be treated as immoral or illegal activity to justify police raids, sealing, or harassment.

The Bihar Vigilance Department’s published process says corruption complaints are examined at Secretariat level, with verification, confirmation from the complainant, supporting evidence, and assignment to a vigilance agency for enquiry. If you submit a complaint and hear nothing, keep a copy and send a written follow-up to the same department or agency asking for a receipt or status update; that is a practical step, not a guarantee that the complaint will be monitored. sources.text:
Under Section 7 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (as substituted in 2018), a public servant who obtains, accepts, or attempts to obtain an undue advantage (such as demanding a cash or UPI bribe to refrain from threatening or filing a baseless case) with intent to perform or forbear from performing a public duty improperly or dishonestly commits a punishable offence; if the person demanding money is impersonating an officer, criminal impersonation and extortion offences also apply.

Exact official passage: Section 7. Offence relating to public servant being bribed.—Any public servant who obtains or accepts or attempts to obtain from any person, an undue advantage, with the intention to perform or cause performance of public duty improperly or dishonestly or to forbear or cause forbearance to perform such duty either by himself or by another public servant, shall be punishable with imprisonment which shall not be less than three years.

messages.content: I am from Chorsua village in Nalanda district, Bihar. My grandfather passed away about a month ago, and he owned around 3 acres of agricultural land. He had two sons, my father and my uncle. Since his death, my uncle has been constantly harassing my father, claiming that the entire land belongs to him because he took care of my grandfather in his final years. My father wants his rightful share, but my uncle is refusing to divide the land. What should we do?

You say your grandfather owned about three acres in Chorsua, had two sons—your father and uncle—and died about a month ago; your uncle is refusing to divide the land.

**Your father should first confirm who legally inherited the land and what the land records show; don't assume the two sons automatically receive half each.** The answer can change if your grandfather left a will, if other heirs are alive, or depending on the type of ownership and the applicable succession law.

---

### What I'd suggest

1. If the Hindu Succession Act applies and the relevant Class I succession rules govern the estate, its text provides for a share for each surviving son and daughter and the deceased's mother, and one share for the widow or widows together; other heirs may also affect the division. [1](#cite-1)

2. For Bihar land records, your father can apply for mutation at the Circle Officer's office for the circle where the land is located, or at a camp run by that officer. The state's guidance says a succession application should include proof of the ancestor's death and documents showing that the applicant is a successor; it also describes a mutual partition route that needs the co-sharers' consent. [2](#cite-2)[3](#cite-3)

3. If your uncle will not consent, ask a local property lawyer to review the title and advise your father on seeking a formal partition through the appropriate court. The sources available here confirm the Bihar mutation process, but do not verify the exact forum or procedure for a contested partition in Nalanda.

---

### What you can do today

Your father can gather the old deed or other ownership papers, current land-record extracts, plot and khata details, your grandfather's death certificate, and documents identifying the family members and any will or partition agreement. Keep copies and a dated note of any threats or attempts to block access.

---

### One thing that would help me

Did your grandfather leave a will, and which close family members—including his wife, daughters, and his own mother—were alive when he died?

---

### What I can't confirm yet

I can't confirm your father's exact share or the correct contested-partition forum without knowing whether your grandfather left a will, which succession law applies, who else in the family survived him, and what the land documents say.

---

### When a lawyer would help

Because this is a disputed claim to agricultural land, a local property lawyer can review the title and identify the right partition route; your father should take the land papers, death certificate, and a list of surviving family members.

9. Order of succession among heirs in the Schedule 
Among the heirs specified in the Schedule, those in class I shall take simultaneously and to the 
exclusion of all other heirs; those in the first entry in class II shall be preferred to those in the second 
entry; those in the second entry shall be preferred to those in the third entry; and so on in succession. 
10 Distribution of property among heirs in class I of the Schedule 
The property of an intestate shall be divided among the heirs in class I of the Schedule in accordance 
with the following rules: 
Rule 1-The intestate’s widow, or if there are more widows than one, all the widows together, shall take 
one share. 
Rule 2-The surviving sons and daughters and the mother of the intestate shall each take one share. 
Rule 3-The heirs in the branch of each pre-deceased son or each pre-deceased daughter of the intestate 
shall take between them one share. 
Rule 4-The distribution of the share referred to in Rule 3- 
 (i) among the heirs in the branch of the pre-deceased son shall be so made that his widow (or widows 
together) and the surviving sons and daughters get equal portions; and the branch of his predeceased 
sons gets the same portion; 
 (ii) among the heirs in the branch of the pre-deceased daughter shall be so made that the surviving 
sons and daughters get equal portions.

messages.content: We have my grandfather's death certificate, old land papers, revenue receipts, and some threatening WhatsApp messages. The land is still in my grandfather's name, and as far as we know, he left no will. My grandmother is alive too. Should we approach the police, the Circle Officer, or a court? And what if the police refuse to register an FIR, saying it's just a family land dispute?

**Use different routes for the different problems: your father can report the threats to police; ask the Circle Officer about updating the land records; and get a local property lawyer to advise on a court case if the heirs cannot agree on division.**

---

### What I'd suggest

1. A threat may amount to criminal intimidation if it threatens injury to a person, reputation or property and is intended to cause alarm or force someone to act or not act; whether these WhatsApp messages meet that test depends on their exact wording and context. BNS section 351 sets out that test. [1](#cite-1)

2. Police must record an FIR when the information discloses a cognizable offence; an FIR is not guaranteed just because a family land disagreement exists or a message is described as threatening. The police assess the information against the offence and the facts. [1](#cite-1)[2](#cite-2)

---

### What you can do today

Your father should take the messages and a written complaint to the police station covering the place where the threats happened. In the complaint, state what was said, when, who sent it, why it caused alarm, and whether anyone tried to enter the land, remove crops or force your father to do something. Ask for a receipt or complaint number and, if an FIR is recorded, a free copy.

---

### If that doesn't work

If the station refuses to record information that your father believes discloses a cognizable offence, he can send the complaint in writing by post to the Superintendent of Police for Nalanda. If that does not resolve it, the next step is an application to the local Magistrate under BNSS section 175(3); the cited procedure requires an affidavit and prior compliance with the police-station and SP steps. [3](#cite-3)[4](#cite-4)[5](#cite-5)

---

### Keep these ready

sources.locator: Section 351: Criminal intimidation
sources.text: 351. (1) Whoever threatens another by any means, with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do any act which that person is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of such threat, commits criminal intimidation. Explanation.—A threat to injure the reputation of any deceased person in whom the person threatened is interested, is within this section. Illustration. A, for the purpose of inducing B to resist from prosecuting a civil suit, threatens to burn B’s house. A is guilty of criminal intimidation. (2) Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. (3) Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation by threatening to cause death or grievous hurt, or to cause the destruction of any property by fire, or to cause an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, or to impute unchastity to a woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both. (4) Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation by an anonymous communication, or having taken precaution to conceal the name or abode of the person from whom the threat comes, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, in addition to the punishment provided for the offence under sub-section (1).

sources.locator: Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 (S. 154) / BNSS 2023 (S. 173) & Lalita Kumari (2014) 2 SCC 1
sources.text:
Under Section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (and Section 173 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023), the police are legally required to register a First Information Report (FIR) when information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence. Registration of an FIR is mandatory as established by the Supreme Court Constitution Bench in Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P. (2014), and a copy of the FIR must be given to the informant immediately and free of cost.

Exact official passage: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 of the Code, if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence and no preliminary inquiry is permissible in such a situation. A copy of the information as recorded shall be given forthwith, free of cost, to the informant.
sources.limitations: Affirmed by Constitution Bench in Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P. (2014) 2 SCC 1; statutory obligation continued under Section 173 of Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS). Exceptions: Preliminary inquiry may be conducted only in specific exceptional categories (matrimonial/family disputes, commercial offences, medical negligence, corruption, or cases with abnormal delay > 3 months) before FIR registration Treatment: good_law_editor_verified.

sources.locator: Section 173: Information in cognizable cases
sources.text: 173. (1) Every information relating to the commission of a cognizable offence, irrespective of the area where the offence is committed, may be given orally or by electronic communication to an officer in charge of a police station, and if given— (i) orally, it shall be reduced to writing by him or under his direction, and be read over to the informant; and every such information, whether given in writing or reduced to writing as aforesaid, shall be signed by the person giving it; (ii) by electronic communication, it shall be taken on record by him on being signed within three days by the person giving it, and the substance thereof shall be entered in a book to be kept by such officer in such form as the State Government may by rules prescribe in this behalf: Provided that if the information is given by the woman against whom an offence under section 64, section 65, section 66, section 67, section 68, section 69, section 70, section 71, section 74, section 75, section 76, section 77, section 78, section 79 or section 124 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is alleged to have been committed or attempted, then such information shall be recorded, by a woman police officer or any woman officer: Provided further that— (a) in the event that the person against whom an offence under section 64, section 65, section 66, section 67, section 68, section 69, section 70, section 71, section 74, section 75, section 76, section 77, section 78, section 79 or section 124 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is alleged to have been committed or attempted, is temporarily or permanently mentally or physically disabled, then such information shall be recorded by a police officer, at the residence of the person seeking to report such offence or at a convenient place of such person's choice, in the presence of an interpreter or a special educator, as the case may be; (b) the recording of such information shall be videographed; (c) the police officer shall get the statement of the person recorded by a Magistrate under clause (a) of sub-section (6) of section 183 as soon as possible. (2) A copy of the information as recorded under sub-section (1) shall be given forthwith, free of cost, to the informant or the victim. (3) Without prejudice to the provisions contained in section 175, on receipt of information relating to the commission of any cognizable offence, which is made punishable for three years or more but less than seven years, the officer in charge of the police station may with the prior permission from an officer not below the rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police, considering the nature and gravity of the offence,— (i) proceed to conduct preliminary enquiry to ascertain whether there exists a prima facie case for proceeding in the matter within a period of fourteen days; or (ii) proceed with investigation when there exists a prima facie case. (4) Any person aggrieved by a refusal on the part of an officer in charge of a police station to record the information referred to in sub-section (1), may send the substance of such information, in writing and by post, to the Superintendent of Police concerned who, if satisfied that such information discloses the commission of a cognizable offence, shall either investigate the case himself or direct an investigation to be made by any police officer subordinate to him, in the manner provided by this Sanhita, and such officer shall have all the powers of an officer in charge of the police station in relation to that offence failing which such aggrieved person may make an application to the Magistrate.

sources.locator: Section 175: Police officer’s power to investigate cognizable case
sources.text: 175. (1) Any officer in charge of a police station may, without the order of a Magistrate, investigate any cognizable case which a Court having jurisdiction over the local area within the limits of such station would have power to inquire into or try under the provisions of Chapter XIV: Provided that considering the nature and gravity of the offence, the Superintendent of Police may require the Deputy Superintendent of Police to investigate the case. (2) No proceeding of a police officer in any such case shall at any stage be called in question on the ground that the case was one which such officer was not empowered under this section to investigate. (3) Any Magistrate empowered under section 210 may, after considering the application supported by an affidavit made under sub-section (4) of section 173, and after making such inquiry as he thinks necessary and submission made in this regard by the police officer, order such an investigation as above-mentioned. (4) Any Magistrate empowered under section 210, may, upon receiving a complaint against a public servant arising in course of the discharge of his official duties, order investigation, subject to— (a) receiving a report containing facts and circumstances of the incident from the officer superior to him; and (b) after consideration of the assertions made by the public servant as to the situation that led to the incident so alleged.

sources.title: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
sources.locator: Section 351: Criminal intimidation
sources.text: 351. (1) Whoever threatens another by any means, with any injury to his person, reputation or property, or to the person or reputation of any one in whom that person is interested, with intent to cause alarm to that person, or to cause that person to do any act which he is not legally bound to do, or to omit to do any act which that person is legally entitled to do, as the means of avoiding the execution of such threat, commits criminal intimidation. Explanation.—A threat to injure the reputation of any deceased person in whom the person threatened is interested, is within this section. Illustration. A, for the purpose of inducing B to resist from prosecuting a civil suit, threatens to burn B’s house. A is guilty of criminal intimidation. (2) Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, or with fine, or with both. (3) Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation by threatening to cause death or grievous hurt, or to cause the destruction of any property by fire, or to cause an offence punishable with death or imprisonment for life, or with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, or to impute unchastity to a woman, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to seven years, or with fine, or with both. (4) Whoever commits the offence of criminal intimidation by an anonymous communication, or having taken precaution to conceal the name or abode of the person from whom the threat comes, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years, in addition to the punishment provided for the offence under sub-section (1).
